hook.text: In 2022, a pig heart was transplanted into a human for the first time — the pig had ten genetic modifications.

buildup.text: Pig organs are similar in size to human organs — but three sugar molecules on pig cells trigger instant rejection.

discovery.text: CRISPR knocked out the three sugar genes and added six human immune-compatibility genes — a custom-fit organ.

twist.text: The patient survived two months — a pig virus reactivated in his body, complicating the outcome.

climax.text: Over 100,000 people wait for organ transplants — genetically modified pigs could end the shortage.

punchline.text: Edit a pig, save a human — xenotransplantation is getting closer.

quiz.question: Why must pig organs be genetically modified before transplanting into humans?
options: Pig organs are too large and must be shrunk genetically
Sugar molecules on pig cells trigger immediate immune rejection in humans
Pig organs lack blood vessels and need genetic modification to grow them

details.summary: Xenotransplantation uses organs from genetically modified animals, primarily pigs, for human transplantation. Gene editing removes pig antigens that trigger rejection and pig viruses, while adding human immune compatibility genes.

faq.question: What genetic modifications make pig organs compatible with humans?
faq.answer: Three pig genes producing galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose and other antigens triggering hyperacute rejection are knocked out. Human genes for complement regulation, coagulation compatibility, and immune modulation are inserted. CRISPR inactivates all porcine endogenous retroviruses for safety.

faq.question: How long did the first pig heart transplant patient survive?
faq.answer: David Bennett received a genetically modified pig heart in January 2022 and survived about two months. The heart functioned well initially but ultimately failed. Porcine cytomegalovirus detected in the organ may have contributed. Subsequent cases aim to improve outcomes with better screening.
